justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term view on the underlying asset, likely a major equity index or ETF trading around the 399–405 range. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major scheduled catalysts would dramatically shift the price overnight. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a small positive drift assumption consistent with historical equity risk premiums, rather than any strong directional signal. Essentially, absent compelling evidence of a near-term shock, I defaulted to a mild upward trend as the baseline expectation.

The confidence interval widths grow predictably with time horizon, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that is standard in financial forecasting. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 24 points, implying daily volatility assumptions consistent with a moderate-volatility regime — perhaps annualized volatility in the 15–20% range. By one month, the interval widens to 100 points, capturing not just price volatility but also the compounding uncertainty around macro conditions, earnings developments, and regime shifts that become increasingly relevant over longer horizons.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharper-than-expected jobs report, a Federal Reserve policy surprise, or renewed credit stress in financial markets — could easily breach the lower bound, especially at the one-month horizon. Geopolitical shocks or sudden liquidity events, like those seen in regional banking crises or flash crashes, could cause rapid moves well outside the stated range. On the upside, a strong earnings season, an unexpected dovish pivot by central banks, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could accelerate buying and push prices above the upper bound. My intervals are calibrated for a relatively normal volatility environment, so fat-tail events — which are underrepresented in standard distributional assumptions — remain a genuine source of model risk.
